forces: Soprano, English horn and concert band
performers: Susan Kavinski, soprano; Richard Reed, English horn; United States Navy Concert Band
intro: The world may think the singer dead; she is living quietly in love and song. Susan Kavinski and English-horn soloist Richard Reed bring Mahler’s retreat from the world to the United States Navy Concert Band.

cues.title: Richard Reed’s English horn
cues.text: The English horn begins with a quiet rising phrase, taking its time between the notes. Mahler asks for an extremely slow, restrained opening. Richard Reed is the instrumental soloist here; his melody supplies the first words Susan Kavinski will sing.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Rückert-Lieder, orchestral score, printed pp. 15–16: cor anglais opening and ruhevoll vocal entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/eb/IMSLP22552-PMLP47682-Mahler_-_R%C3%BCckert_Lieder_(orch._score).pdf. Recording credits: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22Ich_bin_der_Welt_abhanden_gekommen%22_from_R%C3%BCckert-Lieder_-_United_States_Navy_Band.ogg. The concert-band arranger and score are unidentified; tempo and vocal details here come from Mahler’s orchestral score.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An August at Maiernigg
cues.text: Mahler dates the first draft 16 August 1901, at Maiernigg by the Wörthersee. The song belongs to the summer before he meets Alma. Its quiet declaration of life in love and music is already complete.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, essay on Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen, autumn 2008, dates the draft and places it before Mahler’s meeting with Alma: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0086596

cues.title: The melody finds words
cues.text: “Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen” — I have slipped away from the world. Kavinski takes up the English horn’s tune, marked “ruhevoll” — peaceful. The poem begins as a simple explanation for a long absence.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 16–17, rehearsal 1: vocal entry and Friedrich Rückert’s first stanza. Our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The world can believe it
cues.text: The world has heard nothing from the singer and may suppose her dead. She is content to let it think so. Mahler allows the second stanza a little more movement, while the vocal line keeps the ease of speech.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 18–21: end of Rückert’s first stanza, second stanza and Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen at rehearsal 4.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The English horn remembers
cues.text: The voice falls silent after “gestorben der Welt” — dead to the world. The English horn takes up a familiar rising phrase. Mahler holds the music back again, leaving a long breath before the last stanza.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 22–23, rehearsal 6: Wieder zurückhaltend and the cor anglais phrase during the vocal rest. Our translation of Rückert’s words.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A place apart
cues.text: “Und ruh’ in einem stillen Gebiet” — and rest in a quiet place. The opening tempo returns, and the voice begins low. Rückert’s final stanza moves from the world’s commotion to the singer’s own heaven, love and song.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 23–24: Tempo I, low vocal entry and Rückert’s final stanza. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Heaven without a crescendo
cues.text: “Ich leb’ allein in meinem Himmel” — I live alone in my heaven. Mahler marks the voice “innig” — intimate — and asks for no increase as the line reaches heaven. The words “in meinem Lieben” — in my loving — are sung twice before the final mention of song.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 24, rehearsal figures 7–8: innig, intimo, Ohne Steigerung, Senza aumentare and repeated words. Rückert’s words as set by Mahler; our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After “in meinem Lied”
cues.text: Kavinski’s last words are “in meinem Lied” — in my song. The English horn remains, taking up the singer’s rising phrase. Mahler lets the final notes settle very softly, with a held chord at the end.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 25, rehearsal 9: final vocal words, cor anglais return, morendo and the final fermata. Our translation. The band arrangement’s individual accompaniment parts are not documented.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The English horn gives the voice words
transitions.to: A · The singer leaves the world
transitions.how: The English horn’s opening phrase returns in the soprano’s low entrance. “Ich bin der Welt” moves at the same unhurried pace, marked ruhevoll. The instrumental melody becomes a person explaining her absence.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 15–16, rehearsal 1. The concert-band recording credits Kavinski and Reed as the two soloists; the arrangement score is unavailable.

transitions.title: A little more room to move
transitions.from: A · The singer leaves the world
transitions.to: B · Let the world think me dead
transitions.how: The word “gestorben” stretches across several notes at the end of the first stanza. The next line begins more freely at Etwas fließender. Its opening words, “Es ist mir auch gar nichts daran gelegen”, shrug off the world’s mistaken conclusion.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 18–19, rehearsal figures 3–4: vocal phrase and Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen. Accompaniment scoring is not transferred to the band arrangement.

transitions.title: The English horn returns between stanzas
transitions.from: B · Let the world think me dead
transitions.to: Link · The English horn holds back
transitions.how: “Gestorben” is repeated before the voice comes to rest on “der Welt”. The English horn returns during the ensuing silence. Wieder zurückhaltend slows its rising phrase, preparing the opening tempo’s return.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed pp. 22–23, rehearsal 6: repeated vocal word, cor anglais and Wieder zurückhaltend. The original score supplies the structural reference for this band version.

transitions.title: The voice returns low and quietly
transitions.from: Link · The English horn holds back
transitions.to: C · A quiet place to live
transitions.how: The English horn finishes its phrase and the soprano begins low at Tempo I. The repeated opening words, “Ich bin”, now lead to “gestorben dem Weltgetümmel”: dead to the world’s commotion. The line then rises towards its quiet resting place.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 23: Tempo I and the third stanza’s vocal line. Our translation of Rückert’s words as set by Mahler.

transitions.title: The voice leaves its melody behind
transitions.from: C · A quiet place to live
transitions.to: Coda · The song outlives its words
transitions.how: The final “Lied” settles on a long note. The English horn takes over with the singer’s familiar rising phrase. Mahler marks the closing pages morendo; the last chord is held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Mahler’s orchestral score, printed p. 25, rehearsal 9: vocal close, cor anglais return, morendo and final fermata. The band’s redistribution of the accompaniment is undocumented.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Arrangement for soprano, English horn solo and concert band; arranger not identified
fields.note: Commons names the Navy Concert Band, a soprano and an English horn but does not name an arranger or edition. Mahler wrote the song for voice with piano or orchestra, so a band performance implies an arrangement. This recording’s chroma estimates read F major, whereas the first-edition orchestral score on IMSLP (22552) is notated in E♭ major; IMSLP lists the song in F major and notes transposed publications. The estimates suggest a possible pitch difference from that edition, but neither the arrangement’s key nor any transposition has been confirmed.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
